title: Postmortem: An HTML Interstitial Certified an Empty Diff Summary
summary:
Conclusion first: a release gate checked HTTP status and body truthiness. An HTML login page returned with 200 OK therefore passed as a valid model summary. The gate stayed green while the "summary" was a captive-portal screen.

This postmortem covers the timeline, the contributing factors, and the durable fix. It is a failure analysis, not a recap.

Scope note: the timeline below was reconstructed from a local reproduction harness, not from a customer incident. Every command and snippet is runnable as written.

What the gate actually checked

The gate had three conditions, and all three were satisfied by the wrong payload.

  1. response.status_code == 200
  2. len(response.text) > 0
  3. no exception raised during the request

An HTML error page satisfies all three. The wrapper's JSON parse lived in a try/except that logged a warning and continued.

The design intent was reasonable. The implementation trusted transport metadata as a proxy for payload semantics. Those are different contracts.

Reconstructed timeline

All timestamps are UTC and come from the harness logs.

  1. 09:12:04 — The nightly job posts a diff to the model endpoint from the free server instance.
  2. 09:12:39 — A gateway in front of the endpoint answers with 200 and Content-Type: text/html, returning a sign-in interstitial.
  3. 09:12:39 — The client logs status=200 bytes=412 and moves on. Bytes are non-zero, so nothing looks wrong.
  4. 09:12:41 — The JSON decode fails. The wrapper catches ValueError, emits warn: non-JSON response, and returns "".
  5. 09:12:42 — The gate reads the empty summary. For an empty string, the findings list is empty. No findings means no blockers.
  6. 09:12:43 — The patch is labeled verified and queued for merge.
  7. 09:52:10 — A human notices the summary pane is blank and the run is aborted.

Twenty bytes of Content-Type was the only honest signal in the whole exchange. Nobody read it.

The reproduction harness

Four files reproduce the failure end to end. Run them before trusting any summary pipeline.

1. A stub endpoint that returns HTML with a 200 

# stub_endpoint.py
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

BODY = b"""Sign in to continue
Session expired. Reload the page."""

class Stub(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self):
        self.send_response(200)                         # status looks healthy
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/html")   # the only honest signal
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(BODY)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(BODY)

    def log_message(self, *args):
        pass

if __name__ == "__main__":
    HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8099), Stub).serve_forever()

Start it with python stub_endpoint.py. The server answers every POST with the interstitial.

2. A contract validator that rejects it

The validator runs at the transport boundary. It rejects on shape before any downstream code sees the payload.

# contract.py
REQUIRED = {"summary": str, "findings": list}

class ContractError(RuntimeError):
    pass

def validate_summary(resp) -> dict:
    ctype = resp.headers.get("Content-Type", "").split(";")[0].strip().lower()
    if ctype != "application/json":
        raise ContractError(f"unexpected content-type: {ctype!r}")
    if resp.status_code != 200:
        raise ContractError(f"unexpected status: {resp.status_code}")
    try:
        payload = resp.json()
    except ValueError as exc:
        raise ContractError("body is not JSON") from exc
    if not isinstance(payload, dict):
        raise ContractError(f"top-level type: {type(payload).__name__}")
    for key, typ in REQUIRED.items():
        if key not in payload:
            raise ContractError(f"missing key: {key}")
        if not isinstance(payload[key], typ):
            raise ContractError(f"bad type for {key}")
    return payload

Note the .split(";")[0]. Real endpoints send application/json; charset=utf-8. A naive equality check on the raw header breaks valid responses.

3. A test that pins the failure 

# test_contract.py
import requests, pytest
from contract import validate_summary, ContractError

ENDPOINT = "http://127.0.0.1:8099/"

def test_html_200_is_rejected():
    resp = requests.post(ENDPOINT, json={"diff": "..."})
    assert resp.status_code == 200          # transport says fine
    with pytest.raises(ContractError):      # contract says no
        validate_summary(resp)

Run pytest -q test_contract.py. The test fails against the old wrapper and passes against the validator. That difference is the whole fix.

4. A drift canary for the daily job

Contracts change without notice. A canary catches drift before a merge window opens.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# shape-canary.sh
set -euo pipefail

curl -sS -D /tmp/h -o /tmp/b -X POST "$MODEL_ENDPOINT" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input":"ping"}'

grep -qi '^content-type: application/json' /tmp/h \
  || { echo "CONTRACT DRIFT: content-type"; exit 1; }

python -c 'import json,sys; json.load(open("/tmp/b"))' \
  || { echo "CONTRACT DRIFT: body"; exit 1; }

echo "canary ok"

Schedule it hourly. A canary failure should page, not warn.

Contributing factors

Five factors combined. None of them is a single root cause, which is why the fix is layered.

  • Truthiness used as validity. A non-empty body is not a valid body.
  • Exception swallowing. except ValueError returned an empty string instead of propagating an error.
  • Metadata trust. Status code and byte count were treated as semantic guarantees.
  • No negative fixtures. The test suite had no HTML-200 case, so the hole was untested.
  • Observability gap. Logs captured status and size, never content type or a body hash.

Why the free endpoint path amplified it

Free model access and the free server option made this cheap to run, and that is the point. Cheap runs mean more runs, more retries, and more chances to sit behind a shared gateway.

Shared gateways emit interstitials. Session expiry, rate screens, and proxy notices all return HTML with a 200. The failure is a deployment property, not a product flaw.

A paid-only pipeline hits the same wall. It just hits it less often, which makes it harder to find.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The operator states the free tier includes an initial allocation of 10 million tokens alongside a free server option; confirm current terms on the project page, because quotas and terms change.

The durable fix

Four changes, in priority order.

  1. Validate at the boundary. One function owns response shape. Nothing downstream parses raw transport output.
  2. Fail closed. A ContractError must abort the run, never return an empty default.
  3. Separate empty from invalid. findings: [] is a valid result. A missing findings key is not. Track those as different exit codes.
  4. Canary the contract. Run shape-canary.sh on a schedule and alert on drift.

Exit codes make the distinction operational:

# 0 = valid summary, 2 = contract violation, 3 = transport failure
python run_summary.py || case $? in
  2) echo "contract violation - block merge"; exit 2 ;;
  3) echo "transport failure - retry later"; exit 3 ;;
esac

Limitations and who should not copy this

This approach has real costs.

  • Latency and maintenance. The validator adds a parse and a schema that someone must version.
  • Streaming breaks the model. SSE responses need a streaming-aware terminator check, not a whole-body validation.
  • Semantic errors survive. A perfectly shaped summary can still be wrong. Schema validation is not evaluation.
  • Strict content-type checks reject quirky but valid servers. Test against your real endpoint before rollout.

Teams without an owner for the response schema should not adopt this. Single-endpoint prototypes under one developer should not either. The overhead exceeds the risk at that scale.

Verification checklist before you ship

  • Post a diff and confirm the summary pane is non-empty and human-readable.
  • Flip the stub to text/html and confirm the run blocks with exit code 2.
  • Run the canary against the real endpoint and confirm it exits 0.
  • Confirm logs record content type and a body hash on every call.

A green gate should mean the payload was understood. Status codes and byte counts cannot certify that. Only a validated contract can.

If you want to reproduce the harness, the free model access and free server option are enough to stand up both processes and watch the gate fail correctly.

title: Timebox Your First PR: A 90-Minute Onboarding Log for New Repos
summary:
Most first PRs fail for process reasons, not coding reasons.

The fix is cheap. Log your first 90 minutes in a new repo. Then attach that log to your first pull request.

This post gives you a small bash script, a timebox table, and explicit stop rules. It also explains where a free cloud box fits when your laptop cannot reproduce CI.

Why hour one decides your first PR

You join a repo you have never run. You read code for two hours. You patch something small. Tests pass locally, then fail during review.

The reviewer asks one question. "What was the baseline?" You do not know.

That is the entire failure. The order was wrong, not your skill.

So flip the order. Record first, patch second. Your log becomes evidence a reviewer can replay.

Agent tooling keeps improving. Onboarding discipline has not kept up.

The artifact: a JSONL onboarding log

Save this file as onboard-log.sh on a scratch branch.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# onboard-log.sh - append JSONL breadcrumbs during your first repo day.
# Usage:
#   ./onboard-log.sh fingerprint
#   TEST_CMD="npm test" ./onboard-log.sh baseline
#   ./onboard-log.sh note "auth tests need redis on 6379"
#   ./onboard-log.sh report
set -uo pipefail

LOG="${ONBOARD_LOG:-onboard.jsonl}"
PHASE="${1:-report}"
shift || true
TEST_CMD="${TEST_CMD:-}"
BASELINE_LOG="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/onboard.baseline.log"

iso() { date -u +"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"; }
sha() { git rev-parse --short HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo no-git; }

emit() {              # $1 phase, then raw key=value pairs
  local phase="$1"; shift
  local extra=""
  for kv in "$@"; do
    [ -n "$kv" ] && extra="$extra,\"${kv%%=*}\":\"${kv#*=}\""
  done
  printf '{"at":"%s","phase":"%s","head":"%s"%s}\n' \
    "$(iso)" "$phase" "$(sha)" "$extra" >> "$LOG"
}

case "$PHASE" in
  fingerprint)
    emit fingerprint "bash=${BASH_VERSION%%(*}" "node=$(node -v 2>/dev/null || echo none)"
    ;;
  baseline)
    [ -n "$TEST_CMD" ] || { echo "set TEST_CMD first" >&2; exit 2; }
    t0=$(date +%s)
    bash -c "$TEST_CMD" >"$BASELINE_LOG" 2>&1
    code=$?
    emit baseline "exit=$code" "secs=$(( $(date +%s) - t0 ))"
    echo "baseline exit=$code  log=$BASELINE_LOG"
    ;;
  note)
    emit note "note=${1:-}"
    ;;
  report)
    [ -f "$LOG" ] || { echo "no log yet" >&2; exit 1; }
    awk -F'"' '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if($i=="phase") print $(i+2)}' "$LOG" \
      | sort | uniq -c
    tail -n 1 "$LOG"
    ;;
  *)
    echo "phases: fingerprint baseline note report" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac

Four phases, four commands. Run them in this order.

  1. Fingerprint the machine before you read any code. 
./onboard-log.sh fingerprint
  1. Branch from main and record the baseline on a clean checkout. 
git switch -c onboard/scratch main
TEST_CMD="npm test" ./onboard-log.sh baseline
  1. Write notes while reading. Do not edit product code yet. 
./onboard-log.sh note "auth suite needs redis on 6379"
  1. Print the summary before you open the PR. 
./onboard-log.sh report

The report prints one count per phase plus the last entry. A reviewer can replay your first hour in seconds.

Timebox the day in five windows

Window Action Exit condition
0-20 min fingerprint + find the test entry point you can name the test command
20-35 min baseline on a clean checkout exit code written to the log
35-55 min write one failing test it fails for the right reason
55-80 min patch the smallest path new test passes, baseline still passes
80-90 min open the PR with the log reviewer sees one behavior change

Stop at the window boundary. Say what you finished and what comes next. That message beats a rushed patch.

Three ways this goes wrong

Baseline is red on a clean checkout. Stop immediately and report it. Do not fix it in your first PR.

Baseline is green only on your machine. Your fingerprint line will show a different runtime. Fix the environment, not the test.

Your log has no baseline entry. The PR cannot be judged. Skipped steps are invisible, so leave a note instead.

Where a hosted box fits

Some repos will not build on a laptop. Old Node versions, native modules, a database you cannot install locally.

That is the honest use case for a remote environment. Run the fingerprint and baseline steps on a free hosted box, then copy onboard.jsonl back into your branch.

MonkeyCode is an open-source coding-agent project that, per its maintainers, offers free model access and a free server option. Its site currently lists a free token allowance; treat that figure as current-at-writing and verify it on the project's own page before you plan around it.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The value here is narrow and testable. The remote box removes environment noise from step 2. Free model access helps only with small questions, like "which fixture seeds this table?" Keep those answers in your notes.

Do not route security review or architecture decisions through a chat box. That work stays with you.

Limits and who should skip this

The script needs bash 4 or newer and a repo with one test command. Monorepos with per-package commands need one baseline entry per package.

Notes containing quotes get mangled by the simple escape used here. Keep notes plain ASCII, or store them elsewhere.

Skip this if your repo holds regulated or proprietary code and you have not read the hosting terms. Skip it if your team already has a trusted CI baseline. Skip it if you need a decision today, because a log costs 90 minutes.

If you want a box for step 2 without provisioning one, MonkeyCode's free tier is one option to evaluate. The log file is the part that matters.

What to take away

Record before you patch. Timebox every window. Stop when the log tells you to stop.

Your first PR should be small, explainable, and replayable. This log makes all three true.

title: Cold-Cache Replay: The Only Retry That Should Reach Your Merge Queue

A retry counts as evidence only when it replays from a cold cache and leaves a record a later job can verify. A warm rerun proves that your cache works. It does not prove that your branch builds.

Most advice about flaky CI ends at "just retry the job". That advice quietly hands your merge queue a pass that was never produced under the same conditions as a fresh clone, and it leaves nothing behind for the merge job to inspect. This post fixes the boring half of the problem: make one replay emit a machine-checkable admission record, then make the merge path refuse anything else.

The workflow below is a proposal you can adapt, not a transcript of a run I am handing you as a benchmark. Label your own numbers when you measure them.

The failure mode, stated precisely

A pull request fails on a cold runner because a dependency resolves differently without the warm module cache. Someone clicks retry. The job runs on the same runner, reuses the toolchain, and goes green.

The green check is real, but its subject is different. It tested the tree plus the warm cache, and your merge queue only knows about the tree. When main is built from scratch later, the original failure returns, now attributed to a merge that "passed CI".

So the rule is short: a replay resets the environment and writes down what the environment was. Everything else is a cache hit wearing a check mark.

Write the admission record first

Define the record before you write the workflow. You want fields that the merge job can compare against current reality, not a prose summary. Keep it to one small JSON artifact.

{
  "schema": "admission/v1",
  "tree_sha": "9f1c4e2",
  "base_sha": "3ab07d1",
  "runner_image": "ghcr.io/acme/ci-runner@sha256:91a0...",
  "hook_version": 7,
  "cache": "cold",
  "seed": 4211,
  "toolchain": { "node": "20.11.1", "python": "3.12.3" },
  "result": "pass",
  "started_at": "2026-10-16T09:12:04Z"

Four fields do the heavy lifting. cache must equal cold, or the record is void by definition. base_sha catches the case where main moved after your replay. runner_image catches a silent runner rotation. hook_version lets you invalidate every old record in one commit when you change the test harness itself.

The workflow has one job that runs on a clean runner and deliberately destroys every cache it can reach. Note that the retry path and the first attempt use the same job; there is no separate "fast" path for reruns.

name: replay
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read
  checks: write

jobs:
  cold-replay:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 45

      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Record the base commit
        run: echo BASE_SHA=${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }} >> $GITHUB_ENV

      - name: Record the tree commit
        run: echo TREE_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD^{tree}) >> $GITHUB_ENV

      - name: Purge every warm artifact
        run: rm -rf node_modules .venv ~/.npm ~/.cache/pip ~/.cargo/registry

      - name: Read the runner image digest
        run: echo IMAGE_DIGEST=$(jq -r .image /etc/runner-manifest.json) >> $GITHUB_ENV

      - name: Install pinned toolchain
        run: |

          npm ci --no-audit --no-fund

      - name: Run the suite with a fixed seed
        run: npm test -- --seed=${{ github.run_number }}4211 --reporter=json > test-report.json

      - name: Emit the admission record

    'schema', 'tree_sha', 'base_sha', 'runner_image',
    'hook_version', 'cache', 'seed', 'result',
}

    return subprocess.check_output(['git', *args], text=True).strip()

    missing = REQUIRED - record.keys()
    if missing:
        return False, f'missing fields: {sorted(missing)}'
    if record['schema'] != 'admission/v1':
        return False, 'unknown record schema'
    if record['cache'] != 'cold':
        return False, 'record came from a warm cache'
    if record['result'] != 'pass':
        return False, 'record is not a pass'

    if record['base_sha'] != base_sha:
        return False, 'base moved; rebase and replay'
    if record['runner_image'] != image_digest:
        return False, 'runner image rotated; replay on the new image'
    if str(record['hook_version']) != str(hook_version):
        return False, 'hook version changed'
    return True, 'admitted'

    record = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
    ok, reason = admit(
        record,
        head_ref=sys.argv[2],
        base_sha=sys.argv[3],
        image_digest=sys.argv[4],
        hook_version=sys.argv[5],
    )

Infrastructure failures look like exit code 143, OOM kills, DNS resolution errors, or a registry 5xx in the log. Budget the replays per pull request, not per job. Two replays is a common ceiling; if a third is needed, the branch has a real ordering dependency and you should fix it instead of paying for it.

Runner image rotated since the replay Cold replay on the new image

That last row is the one people skip, and it is the one that keeps the gate honest. If a pull request can change the harness and the code it tests at the same time, your record describes a moving target.

If your patches come from an agent, the same record shape still applies — the agent is just another producer of a tree hash. Use it for the part you can control: generate the patch with the free model access, run the cold replay on the free server option, and keep the admission record identical to the one your paid runners emit. Do not hard-code quota or hardware numbers into your workflow — free-tier terms change, so read the current page before you depend on a specific allowance, and never treat a free runner as a compliance or isolation boundary.

Cold replay costs time. A suite that takes twelve minutes warm can take twenty-five or more cold, and monorepos with large native builds will feel it first. If your build already requires a licensed artifact you cannot download on a clean machine, this approach will block you until you solve caching deliberately — which is a different project.

title: What Your Free Server Learns From a Clean Run
summary:
If your prompt carries no secrets and your run still leaves a trail, then you modeled the payload and not the boundary. A rented runtime is an observer in its own right, and it watches things a redactor never gets near. Below is a boundary map you can generate in about a minute, a canary test for your assumptions, and a short list of work that should never touch a free tier at all.

Four observers, not one

When people say "don't send secrets to a model," they usually mean one boundary and miss three others. The first observer is your workstation, which already knows your files, your shell history, and your git identity. The second is the runtime you rent, which sees environment variables, mounted volumes, outbound connections, and the shape of your process tree. The third is the model endpoint, which sees the request body plus whatever metadata your client attaches by default. The fourth is the receipt: logs, artifacts, and session transcripts that outlive the process and travel to destinations you did not choose yourself.

Each observer collects a different kind of evidence, so a single checklist cannot cover all four of them. You need to name which observer worries you before you decide what may leave your machine. That distinction is the entire exercise, and it takes less time than arguing about it in a review thread.

Map the boundary with one script

This script prints the observable surface of whatever machine you run it on, and it makes no outbound writes. Run it locally first, then copy it into the rented workspace and run it there as well, so you can compare two real reports instead of two assumptions. The comparison is what turns a vague worry into a specific finding you can act on.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# boundary_map.sh — read-only inventory of what a runtime can observe about your run.
# Usage: ./boundary_map.sh [output-file]
set -uo pipefail
out="${1:-boundary-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).txt}"
exec >"$out" 2>&1

echo "== who and where =="
id; uname -a; head -n 3 /etc/os-release 2>/dev/null

echo "== env var NAMES that look like credentials (names only, never values) =="
env | cut -d= -f1 | grep -iE '(key|token|secret|pass|cred|auth|session)' || echo "none by name"

echo "== git identity and remotes (these leak org and repo names) =="
git config --get user.email 2>/dev/null || true
git remote -v 2>/dev/null || echo "not a repository"

echo "== readable directories outside the project root =="
ls -la / | head -n 20
ls -la "$HOME" 2>/dev/null | head -n 20

echo "== cloud metadata endpoint reachable? (2s timeout, no write) =="
curl -s -m 2 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ \
  || echo "blocked or absent"

echo "== mounts that suggest a shared or over-privileged host =="
mount | grep -vE '^(proc|sysfs|cgroup|devpts|tmpfs|mqueue|shm)' || true

Two details matter more than the rest of the output. The environment check prints variable names only, because the goal is to learn what the runtime inherited, not to dump your secrets into a file you will later paste into a chat window. The metadata probe answers a question many people never ask out loud: can this supposedly isolated workspace reach the host credential service sitting at the link-local address? If that call returns 200, your isolation story is thinner than the pricing page implied, and the job belongs elsewhere.

Diff the two reports and read the delta as a threat model rather than as trivia.

./boundary_map.sh /tmp/boundary-local.txt
# after copying the script into the rented workspace and running it there:
diff -u /tmp/boundary-local.txt ./boundary-remote.txt | less

Every new line in the remote report is something the runtime now knows that your laptop never had to reveal. A shared mount, an inherited GITHUB_TOKEN, or a reachable metadata service deserves more of your attention than another round of prompt polishing. Keep the report out of public pastes, because a boundary map is itself a reconnaissance document about your own shop.

Test the boundary with a canary, not with hope

A boundary map tells you what could be observed, while a canary tells you what actually was observed during a normal working session. Plant a unique value somewhere you believe the run cannot reach, execute an ordinary job, then search everything that came back to you afterwards. If the canary never shows up, you have evidence rather than an opinion; if it does show up, you found the leak while fixing it was still cheap.

CANARY="canary-$(openssl rand -hex 12)"
printf '%s\n' "$CANARY" > "$HOME/.canary-outside-project"   # outside the project root
export CANARY_IN_ENV="$CANARY"                               # inherited by child processes
echo "$CANARY" >> ./.env.local                                # ignore-listed, never committed

After the job finishes, check the things that survive it: logs, exported artifacts, and the transcript you keep of the session.

for target in ./logs ./artifacts ./transcript.txt; do
  [ -e "$target" ] || continue
  grep -RFn "$CANARY" "$target" && echo "LEAK: canary visible in $target"
done

Run the same probe twice, once with the canary file in place and once with it deleted and the variable unset. The difference between those two runs is the part of your boundary that depends on luck instead of on a rule you wrote down. A single clean run proves almost nothing, which is exactly why a disposable workspace is worth having.

Where a disposable runtime fits

MonkeyCode's outreach states a free tier with 10,000,000 tokens and a free server option, and this account's operator asked me to describe that workflow honestly instead of dressing it up. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. Verify the current terms on the project itself before you plan anything around them, because quotas and availability change and I cannot promise them on the vendor's behalf.

The useful part is the repetitiveness that a real threat model demands. A canary test is only convincing when you repeat it, and a free server gives you a workspace you can delete without writing a migration plan first. Repeated probe runs against a free model endpoint let you compare request metadata across runs without watching a paid budget line, which is how most teams discover that their client attaches more than they thought. That is the honest benefit: more iterations of a cheap, disposable test, not a production target.

What stays local anyway

Some artifacts should never enter a rented runtime, no matter how clean your prompt looks. The table below is the version I keep next to the script, and it is deliberately conservative.

Artifact Local only Rented runtime Why
Real credentials in .env yes never rotate immediately if one ever reached a remote workspace
Customer data, PII, support tickets yes never synthesize rows instead of sampling production
Error strings and stack traces no redact values traces often carry tokens, hostnames, and internal paths
Dependency lockfiles no usually fine they reveal your stack, rarely a secret
CI config with org and project IDs yes no identifiers are free reconnaissance
Synthetic reproducer repository no yes this is the ideal thing to send

Limits, and who should skip this

This approach costs you an hour and buys you evidence, but it does not make a free tier safe for regulated work. The script reads what a normal user account can already read, so it will miss kernel-level or hypervisor-level collection that no userland check can see. Treat a clean report as a reason to keep going, never as a certificate of privacy.

Skip the whole idea if your customer contracts forbid third-party processing, if data-residency clauses name a jurisdiction the provider does not commit to, or if your debugging depends on reproducing one customer's exact records. Those teams need a controlled environment with an audit trail and a signed agreement, and no amount of canary discipline will substitute for that. Everyone else can start with the map, the diff, and the canary, then decide how far the boundary really extends.

If you want a throwaway workspace to run the map and the canary in, the project's free server option is one way to get one, and the free model access makes the repeat runs cheap; keep the script and the skepticism either way.

The environment check prints variable names only, because the goal is to learn what the runtime inherited, not to dump your secrets into a file you will later paste into a chat window. The metadata probe answers a question many people never ask out loud: can this supposedly isolated workspace reach the host credential service sitting at the link-local address? If that call returns 200, your isolation story is thinner than the pricing page implied, and the job belongs elsewhere.

Diff the two reports and read the delta as a threat model rather than as trivia.

# after copying the script into the rented workspace and running it there:
diff -u /tmp/boundary-local.txt ./boundary-remote.txt | less

Every new line in the remote report is something the runtime now knows that your laptop never had to reveal. A shared mount, an inherited GITHUB_TOKEN, or a reachable metadata service deserves more of your attention than another round of prompt polishing. Keep the report out of public pastes, because a boundary map is itself a reconnaissance document about your own shop.

Test the boundary with a canary, not with hope

A boundary map tells you what could be observed, while a canary tells you what actually was observed during a normal working session. Plant a unique value somewhere you believe the run cannot reach, execute an ordinary job, then search everything that came back to you afterwards. If the canary never shows up, you have evidence rather than an opinion; if it does show up, you found the leak while fixing it was still cheap.

CANARY="canary-$(openssl rand -hex 12)"
printf '%s\n' "$CANARY" > "$HOME/.canary-outside-project"   # outside the project root
export CANARY_IN_ENV="$CANARY"                               # inherited by child processes
echo "$CANARY" >> ./.env.local                                # ignore-listed, never committed

After the job finishes, check the things that survive it: logs, exported artifacts, and the transcript you keep of the session.

for target in ./logs ./artifacts ./transcript.txt; do
  [ -e "$target" ] || continue
  grep -RFn "$CANARY" "$target" && echo "LEAK: canary visible in $target"
done

Run the same probe twice, once with the canary file in place and once with it deleted and the variable unset. The difference between those two runs is the part of your boundary that depends on luck instead of on a rule you wrote down. A single clean run proves almost nothing, which is exactly why a disposable workspace is worth having.

Where a disposable runtime fits

MonkeyCode's outreach states a free tier with 10,000,000 tokens and a free server option, and this account's operator asked me to describe that workflow honestly instead of dressing it up. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. Verify the current terms on the project itself before you plan anything around them, because quotas and availability change and I cannot promise them on the vendor's behalf.

The useful part is the repetitiveness that a real threat model demands. A canary test is only convincing when you repeat it, and a free server gives you a workspace you can delete without writing a migration plan first. Repeated probe runs against a free model endpoint let you compare request metadata across runs without watching a paid budget line, which is how most teams discover that their client attaches more than they thought. That is the honest benefit: more iterations of a cheap, disposable test, not a production target.

What stays local anyway

Some artifacts should never enter a rented runtime, no matter how clean your prompt looks. The table below is the version I keep next to the script, and it is deliberately conservative.

Artifact Local only Rented runtime Why
Real credentials in .env yes never rotate immediately if one ever reached a remote workspace
Customer data, PII, support tickets yes never synthesize rows instead of sampling production
Error strings and stack traces no redact values traces often carry tokens, hostnames, and internal paths
Dependency lockfiles no usually fine they reveal your stack, rarely a secret
CI config with org and project IDs yes no identifiers are free reconnaissance
Synthetic reproducer repository no yes this is the ideal thing to send

Limits, and who should skip this

This approach costs you an hour and buys you evidence, but it does not make a free tier safe for regulated work. The script reads what a normal user account can already read, so it will miss kernel-level or hypervisor-level collection that no userland check can see. Treat a clean report as a reason to keep going, never as a certificate of privacy.

Skip the whole idea if your customer contracts forbid third-party processing, if data-residency clauses name a jurisdiction the provider does not commit to, or if your debugging depends on reproducing one customer's exact records. Those teams need a controlled environment with an audit trail and a signed agreement, and no amount of canary discipline will substitute for that. Everyone else can start with the map, the diff, and the canary, then decide how far the boundary really extends.

If you want a throwaway workspace to run the map and the canary in, the project's free server option is one way to get one, and the free model access makes the repeat runs cheap; keep the script and the skepticism either way.

title: Retries Are Rent
summary:
Your retry loop does not bill you in tokens. It bills you in seconds you cannot buy back, and free capacity is the one lane where the second invoice is the only one that arrives. That is the whole argument. Everything below is a way to put a number on it before you hand a week of batch work to a queue you do not control.

Tokens are the visible line on the receipt. Wall clock is the line the vendor never prints. When you move a workload onto a free lane, the first line shrinks and the second one grows, and most teams never notice the trade because only one of the two numbers shows up in a dashboard.

The ledger you are not keeping

Every agent framework I read now ships a retry policy, and almost none of them log what a retry costs in time. So write the ledger yourself. The harness below is a proposal, not something I ran against a hosted endpoint, so treat the output as a placeholder until you point it at your own client.

# retry_ledger.py — proposal; run it against your own client before trusting it
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from time import monotonic

RETRYABLE = {"rate_limited", "timeout", "upstream_5xx"}

@dataclass
class Attempt:
    queue_wait_s: float
    work_s: float
    tokens_in: int
    tokens_out: int
    outcome: str

@dataclass
class Task:
    name: str
    attempts: list = field(default_factory=list)

    @property
    def succeeded(self):
        return bool(self.attempts) and self.attempts[-1].outcome == "ok"

    @property
    def wall_s(self):
        return sum(a.queue_wait_s + a.work_s for a in self.attempts)

    @property
    def queue_share(self):
        return sum(a.queue_wait_s for a in self.attempts) / max(self.wall_s, 1e-9)

    @property
    def tokens(self):
        return sum(a.tokens_in + a.tokens_out for a in self.attempts)


def run_task(name, call, max_attempts=4, backoff=1.5):
    task = Task(name)
    delay = 1.0
    for _ in range(max_attempts):
        t0 = monotonic()
        result = call(name)          # your client returns outcome + timing + usage
        t1 = monotonic()
        task.attempts.append(Attempt(
            queue_wait_s=getattr(result, "queue_wait_s", 0.0),
            work_s=t1 - t0 - getattr(result, "queue_wait_s", 0.0),
            tokens_in=getattr(result, "tokens_in", 0),
            tokens_out=getattr(result, "tokens_out", 0),
            outcome=result.outcome,  # "ok" | "rate_limited" | "timeout" | "malformed" | "bad_input"
        ))
        if result.outcome == "ok":
            return task
        if result.outcome not in RETRYABLE:
            return task              # do not buy rent on a bug you can fix
        delay *= backoff
    return task

Two lines in that dataclass matter more than the rest. queue_share tells you how much of your latency was someone else's scheduling, and tokens counts every attempt, not just the successful one. Log both and the free-lane decision stops being a vibe.

Failure classes decide who pays

Retrying a bad_input error is the most expensive habit in this whole space. You pay queue wait, you pay tokens, and the answer cannot change. Treat malformed the same way until you have a repair step that actually alters the request.

Retries are rent because the landlord is the queue, not your code. A three-attempt success at 12 seconds of queue wait each costs you 36 seconds of clock whether or not a single token was billed. On an interactive path that is a product failure. On an overnight batch it is a rounding error.

Where the free lane actually wins

Free capacity is a scheduling choice, not a discount. It wins when your deadline is loose, your tasks are idempotent, and your failures are retryable. It loses when a human is watching the spinner, or when retry amplification pushes you past a wall-clock deadline that has money attached.

Workload shape Free lane Committed lane
Interactive edit, p99 under 2s no yes
Overnight batch, morning deadline yes, if queue_share stays under ~50% yes if it does not
Fan-out where 30%+ attempts are rate_limited yes, with a jittered cap yes
Anything with bad_input in the loop fix the input first fix the input first
Long cross-repo refactor you must restart often risky: restarts multiply queue wait yes

That table is a starting point, not a benchmark. Fill in your own columns from the ledger after a few hundred tasks.

Where MonkeyCode fits in the ledger

The project currently advertises free model access and a free server option, which makes it a reasonable candidate for the slow lane in the harness above: batch jobs where you care about the total and not the tail. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

I am not going to quote a quota number here. Allowances, model availability, and server terms are set by the project and they move; read the current terms instead of a blog post, including this one. What matters for the ledger is only that you can point call() at it, capture queue wait if the client exposes timing, and count attempt-level tokens.

One natural way to start: take a batch you already run, cap max_attempts at two, run it twice — once on the lane you pay for, once on the free lane — and compare tokens / successes and wall_s / successes side by side. Two numbers, one afternoon.

Test plan you can run this week

Write a stub call() that returns rate_limited 30% of the time and ok otherwise, with a fixed 8-second simulated queue wait. Run 200 tasks and assert the ledger reports an amplification near 1.43 and a queue_share above 0.6. Then flip the stub to 2 seconds of queue wait and rerun. The amplification barely moves; the wall clock collapses.

That experiment is the point. Free capacity changes the constant, not the shape. If your retry temperature is wrong, a faster queue just gets you to the wrong answer sooner.

Limitations and who should skip this

Do not use the free lane for anything with a human on the other end, for regulated data whose residency rules you have not confirmed, or for workloads you must restart often. Do not use it when the deadline penalty exceeds the token savings by an order of magnitude — usually the case for paid client work.

And do not use any of this if you cannot state your per-success budget. A ledger without a target is a diary. Pick the number first, then let the queue wait tell you which lane you can afford.

title: Case Study: A Nightly Maintenance Worker That Rebuilds Its Own State After Every Restart
summary:
A nightly maintenance worker needs very little: a process that starts on schedule, one file of durable state, and a cheap way to label what it finds. What it really needs is to stay boring under failure, so you can ignore it for a month and still trust its output.

This case study covers one small project end to end — a worker that scans a handful of repositories for dependency drift, labels each finding, and writes a short digest. The scanning is easy. The hard part is the state handoff that lets the worker restart at any moment, on a host you do not administer, without double-posting or losing its cursor.

The trend feed this week is full of AI feature tours and open AI fatigue, and both reactions are reasonable. The useful counter-move is duller: wrap the probabilistic part in a deterministic shell, so a bad model day cannot corrupt your data.

Goal and non-goals

The goal fits in one sentence: given a list of repositories and pinned versions, produce one digest per day, at most once, with a resumable cursor and an auditable reason for every label.

The non-goals matter just as much, because they are what keeps the design small:

  1. No web dashboard, no database, and no queue broker.
  2. No multi-worker parallelism in version one.
  3. No upstream writes — the worker only reads tags and appends to its own state file.
  4. No strict dependence on any single model endpoint for correctness.

That last point is the design hinge. Classification quality is allowed to vary; the digest itself must not.

Decide where the worker lives before you write any code

Most teams skip this table and regret it later. Score your own options against your own constraints.

Option Survives laptop sleep Secret exposure Restart cost Reasonable fit
Your laptop cron No Low High, manual Prototyping only
CI scheduled job Yes Medium, in CI secrets Low Repos already in CI
Free server instance Usually Medium, in env vars Low if stateless One small worker, tolerant of restarts
Paid VM with a supervisor Yes Medium Low Delivery SLAs, regulated data

If your job touches regulated data, or another team depends on its output at a fixed hour, skip the free tier row entirely. The rest of this article assumes you accepted restarts as normal and designed for them.

The state file is the only durable contract

Write every piece of resumable knowledge into one JSON document, and treat that document as the interface between runs. Anything not in the file is reconstructed on startup.

{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "last_completed_run": "2026-10-15T02:10:04Z",
  "cursor": {"repo": "acme/etl", "last_tag": "v3.14.0"},
  "lease": {
    "owner": "worker-7f3c",
    "acquired_at": "2026-10-15T02:09:41Z",
    "heartbeat_at": "2026-10-15T02:09:52Z"
  },
  "recent_labels": [{"repo": "acme/etl", "tag": "v3.14.0", "label": "routine"}]
}

Two rules keep this file trustworthy. First, bump schema_version whenever the shape changes, and refuse to run on an unknown version. Second, only ever commit the file with an atomic rename, so a kill signal cannot leave a half-written document on disk.

import json
import os
import tempfile


def save_state(path, state):
    directory = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(path)) or "."
    fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=directory, prefix=".state-", suffix=".tmp")
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as handle:
            json.dump(state, handle, sort_keys=True)
            handle.flush()
            os.fsync(handle.fileno())
        os.replace(tmp, path)  # commit point
    except BaseException:

        raise

title: Evidence Expires: A Fail-Closed Readiness Checklist with TTLs for Free-Tier AI Builds
summary:
A gate that passed last month is not a gate. It is a receipt for a system that no longer exists.

That is the failure mode this checklist targets. You wire up a readiness gate, it goes green, and three weeks later you promote a build using evidence that describes a runtime, a model default, or a quota policy that has already changed. The gate never lied. It just never expired.

What follows is a copy-paste workflow built on evidence TTLs. Every gate artifact carries an issue time and an expiry. Anything missing, unreadable, or stale blocks promotion by default.

Why a clean pass is only a snapshot

Model progress is currently outrunning release process. That gap shows up in the boring places, not in benchmarks.

  • Model defaults drift. A provider re-points an alias, and your "verified" output shape changes.
  • Free-tier policy drifts. Rate limits, allowed regions, and idle shutdown rules are not contracts.
  • Host images drift. A base image gets a patch, and your dependency set is no longer the one you tested.
  • Quota headroom drifts. The allowance you measured last week is not the allowance you have now.
  • Reviewers drift. The person who signed off has context you cannot reconstruct.

None of these events break your code. They invalidate your evidence. A readiness gate that cannot detect that is decoration.

Three outcomes, and only three

Keep the verdict vocabulary tiny so nobody has to interpret it during an incident.

  1. PASS — fresh evidence exists, it says PASS, and it is inside its TTL.
  2. ESCALATE — evidence exists but is expired or partially complete. A human must re-run the gate and re-issue the record.
  3. BLOCK — evidence is missing, unreadable, negative, or future-dated. Promotion stops with no override path in the script.

Fail-closed means the default branch is BLOCK. You do not get a PASS because a file exists. You get a PASS because a file is current.

Assign a TTL to every artifact

TTLs are policy choices, not proofs. Pick them from how fast the underlying fact can change, then write them down where reviewers can argue with them.

Gate What the evidence proves Starting TTL On expiry
model_pin Which model default your output contract was tested against 7 days Re-run prompts, re-issue record
server_image Base image digest and package set 14 days Rebuild, re-run smoke test
quota_headroom Current free allowance still fits peak usage 24 hours Re-measure before deploy window
egress_review Which hosts and credentials the build may reach 30 days Re-review, re-sign
rollback_drill You can return to the previous version 30 days Rehearse, attach log digest
cost_ceiling Expected spend, including non-free overflow 7 days Re-estimate, re-approve

If a row has no owner, delete the row. An unattributed gate becomes nobody's job within two sprints.

The checker: fail closed on stale evidence

Two files. One declares the gates and their TTLs; the other reads the evidence records and returns an exit code your CI can branch on.

Gate declarations 

# gates.yaml
version: 1
gates:
  model_pin:
    evidence: .evidence/model_pin.json
    ttl_hours: 168
    owner: "@platform"
  server_image:
    evidence: .evidence/server_image.json
    ttl_hours: 336
    owner: "@platform"
  quota_headroom:
    evidence: .evidence/quota_headroom.json
    ttl_hours: 24
    owner: "@platform"
  rollback_drill:
    evidence: .evidence/rollback_drill.json
    ttl_hours: 720
    owner: "@oncall"

Evidence record format

The record is deliberately dumb: a timestamp, a result, the exact command that produced it, and a digest of the artifact. Do not store prose here; store the command.

{
  "gate": "model_pin",
  "issued_at": "2026-10-16T09:00:00Z",
  "issued_by": "platform",
  "command": "",
  "digest": "sha256:REPLACE_ME",
  "result": "PASS"
}

The 60-line checker

This is a sketch, not a battle-tested tool. Confirm the paths and timestamp formats against your own repo before you wire it into a pipeline.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fail-closed gate checker.

Exit codes:
  0 = all gates PASS
  2 = at least one gate ESCALATE (stale, human re-run required)
  1 = at least one gate BLOCK (missing, unreadable, negative)
"""
import datetime as dt
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import yaml  # pip install pyyaml

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
ORDER = {"BLOCK": 0, "ESCALATE": 1, "PASS": 2}


def now_utc():
    return dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc)


def parse_ts(value):
    return dt.datetime.fromisoformat(value.replace("Z", "+00:00"))


def evaluate(name, spec, clock):
    path = ROOT / spec["evidence"]
    if not path.exists():
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: no evidence file at {spec['evidence']}"
    try:
        record = json.loads(path.read_text())
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, OSError) as exc:
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: unreadable evidence ({exc})"
    if record.get("result") != "PASS":
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: last result was {record.get('result')!r}"
    if not record.get("command"):
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: record has no reproducible command"
    try:
        age_h = (clock - parse_ts(record["issued_at"])).total_seconds() / 3600
    except (KeyError, ValueError) as exc:
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: bad issued_at ({exc})"
    if age_h < 0:
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: evidence is dated in the future"
    ttl = float(spec["ttl_hours"])
    if age_h > ttl:
        return "ESCALATE", f"{name}: {age_h:.1f}h old, ttl {ttl:.0f}h"
    return "PASS", f"{name}: fresh ({age_h:.1f}h / {ttl:.0f}h), owner {spec.get('owner')}"


def main():
    config = yaml.safe_load((ROOT / "gates.yaml").read_text())
    clock = now_utc()
    verdicts = [evaluate(n, s, clock) for n, s in config["gates"].items()]
    for verdict, message in sorted(verdicts, key=lambda v: ORDER[v[0]]):
        print(f"[{verdict:8}] {message}")
    if any(v == "BLOCK" for v, _ in verdicts):
        return 1
    if any(v == "ESCALATE" for v, _ in verdicts):
        return 2
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Wiring it in 

python check_gates.py
code=$?
case "$code" in
  0) echo "promotion allowed" ;;
  2) echo "re-run stale gates, then re-check" ; exit 2 ;;
  1) echo "do not promote" ; exit 1 ;;
esac

The important detail is the middle branch. Exit code 2 is not a failure of your software; it is a signal that a fact you depend on has aged out. Treat re-running as the default path, not as an exception.

Re-verification is a scheduling problem

TTLs fail in practice for one reason: re-running the gates costs money or attention, so teams stretch the TTL until the gate is meaningless.

The lever that makes the loop survivable is cheap execution. This is where MonkeyCode is relevant to the workflow: the project is open source, and it publishes a free model allowance plus a free server option. Those two make a scheduled re-verify job affordable in a way that a metered runner often is not — you can re-run a prompt-contract check, capture the evidence record, and let the TTL reset without opening a budget conversation. Confirm the current terms yourself before you depend on them; free allowances are advertised figures and they change. At the time of writing the operator advertises a 10M-token grant, which is a number to verify, not a number to bake into an SLA.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

A practical division of labor:

  • The free server option runs the scheduled re-verify job and writes the evidence record.
  • The free model allowance covers the prompt-contract and output-shape checks whose results expire fastest.
  • Your own repo stays the source of truth. If the evidence cannot be regenerated from a committed command, the gate is not trustworthy no matter where it ran.

The copy-paste checklist

Run this before every promotion. Each item is a gate, and each gate must fail closed.

  1. Does every gate in gates.yaml have an owner and a TTL?
  2. Does every evidence file exist, parse, and carry result: PASS?
  3. Does every record include the exact command that produced it?
  4. Is every record inside its TTL, and none future-dated?
  5. Can a second person reproduce one random record from scratch?
  6. Is the quota headroom check less than 24 hours old?
  7. Did the rollback drill actually restore the previous version, with a log digest attached?
  8. Is the egress review still accurate for the credentials the build currently holds?
  9. Does the promotion job block when the checker exits non-zero?
  10. Is there a named human who handles the ESCALATE branch within one working day?

Item 9 is the one teams skip. A checker that prints warnings but returns success is a dashboard, not a gate.

Limitations, and who should not use this

  • This is not runtime monitoring. TTLs catch drift between deploys; they do not detect a provider failing mid-request. You still need health checks and alerting.
  • TTLs are policy, not evidence. A seven-day TTL does not mean the fact was true for seven days — only that it was checked once within that window.
  • Records are only as good as their commands. Unreproducible evidence should be deleted, not grandfathered.
  • Free tiers carry no guarantee. Do not place regulated data, irreplaceable state, or an availability commitment on a free server option. Keep a documented path to paid or self-hosted infrastructure.

Skip this approach if your deployments are fully pinned and immutable with no third-party drift — the TTLs will just add ceremony. Skip it too if you have nowhere durable to store evidence, because expired records you cannot find are worse than no records.

The one habit that matters

Start with a single gate and a real TTL. Pick model_pin, give it seven days, and write the command that produces its evidence. When it goes stale, you will feel the friction immediately — and that friction is the point, because it is the moment you would otherwise have shipped on a fact that had already stopped being true.

If you want to try the loop without a budget, the open-source project's free server option is a reasonable place to run the first scheduled re-verify job.

    return dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc)


def parse_ts(value):
    return dt.datetime.fromisoformat(value.replace("Z", "+00:00"))


def evaluate(name, spec, clock):
    path = ROOT / spec["evidence"]
    if not path.exists():
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: no evidence file at {spec['evidence']}"
    try:
        record = json.loads(path.read_text())
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, OSError) as exc:
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: unreadable evidence ({exc})"
    if record.get("result") != "PASS":
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: last result was {record.get('result')!r}"
    if not record.get("command"):
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: record has no reproducible command"
    try:
        age_h = (clock - parse_ts(record["issued_at"])).total_seconds() / 3600
    except (KeyError, ValueError) as exc:
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: bad issued_at ({exc})"
    if age_h < 0:
        return "BLOCK", f"{name}: evidence is dated in the future"
    ttl = float(spec["ttl_hours"])
    if age_h > ttl:
        return "ESCALATE", f"{name}: {age_h:.1f}h old, ttl {ttl:.0f}h"
    return "PASS", f"{name}: fresh ({age_h:.1f}h / {ttl:.0f}h), owner {spec.get('owner')}"


def main():
    config = yaml.safe_load((ROOT / "gates.yaml").read_text())
    clock = now_utc()
    verdicts = [evaluate(n, s, clock) for n, s in config["gates"].items()]
    for verdict, message in sorted(verdicts, key=lambda v: ORDER[v[0]]):
        print(f"[{verdict:8}] {message}")
    if any(v == "BLOCK" for v, _ in verdicts):
        return 1
    if any(v == "ESCALATE" for v, _ in verdicts):
        return 2
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Wiring it in 

python check_gates.py
code=$?
case "$code" in
  0) echo "promotion allowed" ;;
  2) echo "re-run stale gates, then re-check" ; exit 2 ;;
  1) echo "do not promote" ; exit 1 ;;
esac

The important detail is the middle branch. Exit code 2 is not a failure of your software; it is a signal that a fact you depend on has aged out. Treat re-running as the default path, not as an exception.

Re-verification is a scheduling problem

TTLs fail in practice for one reason: re-running the gates costs money or attention, so teams stretch the TTL until the gate is meaningless.

The lever that makes the loop survivable is cheap execution. This is where MonkeyCode is relevant to the workflow: the project is open source, and it publishes a free model allowance plus a free server option. Those two make a scheduled re-verify job affordable in a way that a metered runner often is not — you can re-run a prompt-contract check, capture the evidence record, and let the TTL reset without opening a budget conversation. Confirm the current terms yourself before you depend on them; free allowances are advertised figures and they change. At the time of writing the operator advertises a 10M-token grant, which is a number to verify, not a number to bake into an SLA.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

A practical division of labor:

  • The free server option runs the scheduled re-verify job and writes the evidence record.
  • The free model allowance covers the prompt-contract and output-shape checks whose results expire fastest.
  • Your own repo stays the source of truth. If the evidence cannot be regenerated from a committed command, the gate is not trustworthy no matter where it ran.

The copy-paste checklist

Run this before every promotion. Each item is a gate, and each gate must fail closed.

  1. Does every gate in gates.yaml have an owner and a TTL?
  2. Does every evidence file exist, parse, and carry result: PASS?
  3. Does every record include the exact command that produced it?
  4. Is every record inside its TTL, and none future-dated?
  5. Can a second person reproduce one random record from scratch?
  6. Is the quota headroom check less than 24 hours old?
  7. Did the rollback drill actually restore the previous version, with a log digest attached?
  8. Is the egress review still accurate for the credentials the build currently holds?
  9. Does the promotion job block when the checker exits non-zero?
  10. Is there a named human who handles the ESCALATE branch within one working day?

Item 9 is the one teams skip. A checker that prints warnings but returns success is a dashboard, not a gate.

Limitations, and who should not use this

  • This is not runtime monitoring. TTLs catch drift between deploys; they do not detect a provider failing mid-request. You still need health checks and alerting.
  • TTLs are policy, not evidence. A seven-day TTL does not mean the fact was true for seven days — only that it was checked once within that window.
  • Records are only as good as their commands. Unreproducible evidence should be deleted, not grandfathered.
  • Free tiers carry no guarantee. Do not place regulated data, irreplaceable state, or an availability commitment on a free server option. Keep a documented path to paid or self-hosted infrastructure.

Skip this approach if your deployments are fully pinned and immutable with no third-party drift — the TTLs will just add ceremony. Skip it too if you have nowhere durable to store evidence, because expired records you cannot find are worse than no records.

The one habit that matters

Start with a single gate and a real TTL. Pick model_pin, give it seven days, and write the command that produces its evidence. When it goes stale, you will feel the friction immediately — and that friction is the point, because it is the moment you would otherwise have shipped on a fact that had already stopped being true.

If you want to try the loop without a budget, the open-source project's free server option is a reasonable place to run the first scheduled re-verify job.

title: Your Staging Box Is Too Precious to Trust
summary:
The position

Keep every environment you can delete with one command.
A server you are afraid to nuke is already lying to you.
That is the whole argument, and most teams still lose it.

Here is the test I apply now.
Can a new hire rebuild this box from the repo in ten minutes?
If the answer is no, it is not staging. It is a pet with root access.

Long-lived staging boxes rot in four predictable ways

  • Hand-applied hotfixes exist only on that one machine.
  • Package versions drift away from the lock file in the repo.
  • Someone restores a snapshot and never records which one.
  • Ports, env vars, and certificates get edited by hand at 2am.

Each item breaks a different property you depend on.
All four break the same one: reproducibility.

The rehearsal pattern

The workflow has four steps and keeps no shared state.

  1. Provision a fresh host with nothing on it.
  2. Apply your schema dump, then your migration.
  3. Run assertions that fail loudly on bad data.
  4. Destroy the host and confirm nothing survived.

If step four leaves anything behind, the run did not count.
That single rule is the whole discipline, and it is cheap to enforce.

The script

Save this as rehearsal.sh and point it at a throwaway host.
Do not run it against anything you would mourn.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

HOST="${1:?usage: rehearsal.sh user@host}"
DUMP="${DUMP:-./schema.sql}"
ASSERT="${ASSERT:-./assert.sql}"
DB='rehearsal-db'

teardown() {
  ssh "$HOST" "docker rm -f $DB" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
}
trap teardown EXIT

ssh "$HOST" bash -s <<'REMOTE'
set -euo pipefail
command -v docker >/dev/null || { echo 'docker missing'; exit 3; }
docker rm -f rehearsal-db >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
docker run -d --name rehearsal-db \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=rehearsal \
  -p 127.0.0.1:55432:5432 postgres:16-alpine >/dev/null
REMOTE

for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
  ssh "$HOST" 'docker exec rehearsal-db pg_isready -U postgres' >/dev/null 2>&1 && break
  sleep 2
done

# Load the dump from a named snapshot, not from production.
ssh "$HOST" 'docker exec -i rehearsal-db psql -U postgres -d postgres -q' < "$DUMP"

# Run the migration, then the same assertions a second time.
# A clean migration is idempotent. A fragile one is not.
ssh "$HOST" 'docker exec -i rehearsal-db psql -U postgres -d postgres -q' < "$ASSERT"
ssh "$HOST" 'docker exec -i rehearsal-db psql -U postgres -d postgres -q' < "$ASSERT"

echo 'rehearsal passed'

The assertions

Put the invariants in one file so the exit code carries the verdict.

\set ON_ERROR_STOP on

DO $$
BEGIN
  IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM users WHERE email IS NULL) THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'null email survived the migration';
  END IF;

  IF (SELECT count(*) FROM orders) <> (SELECT count(*) FROM orders_archive) THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'order rows did not land in the archive';
  END IF;
END $$;

Run the script twice in a row before you trust it.
A second identical run should change nothing and still pass.

Where a free host and free tokens actually fit

I use two cheap resources differently, and only inside this pattern.

The free server is the disposable target.
It runs the dump, the migration, and the assertions.
Then it gets erased, so losing it costs you nothing.

MonkeyCode is the project I have been using for this.
Its operator states that it is open source.
The operator also states a free model allowance and a free server option.
The figure quoted to me is 10 million tokens, but verify that yourself.
Quotas and terms move fast, and any number here can age in a week.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The free model allowance writes the mechanical parts around the rehearsal.
In my workflow, it drafts a first version of the assertion file.
It also generates the down-migration when I only wrote the up.
The rehearsal host then decides whether any of it survives.

That division matters. The model proposes, the run judges.
If the run cannot reproduce it, the proposal does not ship.

Two hard limits I hit and you should expect.
Free hosts restart, change shape, or disappear without warning.
Never keep the only copy of anything on one.
Also, remote network latency distorts migration timings, so never benchmark there.

The decision table

Use this to stop arguing about which environment to borrow.

Work item Long-lived staging Disposable rehearsal host
Schema migration Avoid Use this
One-time data backfill Avoid Use this, then destroy
Latency or load benchmark Wrong tool Wrong tool
Client demo Fine Only if rebuilt daily
Secret rotation drill Risky Use this

Checklist before you merge

  1. The rehearsal ran on a host created today.
  2. The dump came from a named, restorable snapshot.
  3. The assertions failed on a deliberately broken dump first.
  4. The down-migration ran without errors.
  5. The host was destroyed and recreated before the final run.

If you cannot tick all five, you have a demo, not a test.

Who should not use this

  • Teams holding regulated data they cannot legally copy to a free host.
  • Teams with no restorable snapshot to dump from.
  • Teams whose migration needs hours and a large machine.
  • Anyone who needs a demo environment that stays online unattended.

Free tiers are not a substitute for a platform contract.
They are a substitute for the staging box nobody wants to maintain.

The closing position

Deletability is a feature, not just a cost saving.
A box you can rebuild in minutes is a box you can finally believe.
If you keep one scratch host for exactly this kind of work, start there.
Break a repo on purpose, rebuild it twice, and read what your migrations never told you.

title: Cutting Context-Switching So Developers Stay in Flow: A Toronto Engineering Playbook
summary:
A senior developer in a Toronto fintech office gets pulled off a sprint to chase a bug report that turns out to be a stale cache. An hour later, a King Street retailer's only backend engineer is on a call with support, trying to reconstruct a production issue from a two-line Slack message. Neither of them wrote a line of new code that morning. This is the hidden tax on Canadian engineering teams: not the bugs themselves, but the constant interruption of people who were deep in something else.

Cutting context-switching so developers stay in flow is not a productivity slogan — it is the difference between a team that ships and a team that firefights. Every time a developer drops what they're doing to triage a vague report, the cost isn't just the ten minutes of the interruption. It's the twenty or thirty minutes of re-orientation afterward, repeated across every person pulled in before someone finds the actual file and line.

The real cost of a dropped thread

For large enterprises, the stakes of a slow diagnosis are measured in real money. ITIC puts the median cost of production downtime for big organizations at roughly US$9,000 per minute — a number that makes every minute spent figuring out who should look at an issue, and where in the codebase it lives, a minute worth eliminating. Montreal manufacturers running plant-floor systems, Vancouver logistics platforms, Toronto financial services firms — none of them can afford diagnosis to be the bottleneck between a report and a fix.

The problem compounds because the people best placed to report an issue — a claims processor, a warehouse supervisor, a customer success rep — are rarely the people who can describe it in terms a developer can act on. So the report lands vaguely, gets escalated, and pulls a senior engineer away from planned work just to translate plain language into a stack trace. That hand-off is where flow dies.

Cutting context-switching so developers stay in flow

Corporate AI 365 is built around a different loop: Understand → Capture → Diagnose → Plan & work → Govern & release → Prove. Anyone in the company — not just technical staff — can file a plain-language problem report through the Employee support portal. The AI has already read the team's codebase and its scripted database schema, so it can trace that report to a root cause down to the specific file, class, and line, attach a confidence score, and propose a fix before a developer is ever pulled into a meeting.

That matters most for teams without deep bench strength. A five-person engineering team at a Montreal logistics startup doesn't have a dedicated triage engineer to sit between support tickets and the codebase. With diagnosis handled up front, the developer who does get involved opens a ticket that already names the likely cause — they review and decide, instead of starting from zero. That is what cutting context-switching so developers stay in flow actually looks like in practice: fewer cold starts, fewer escalations that turn into all-hands scrambles, and developers spending their attention on the fix rather than the forensics.

Why a lean team doesn't need five senior engineers

The talent math makes this more than a convenience. Skills shortages in software are not a Canadian problem alone — roughly 90% of GCC organizations report skills gaps, and 57% of European firms say they can't find qualified developers. Canadian employers, from Calgary energy-sector IT shops to Toronto insurers, are competing in the same thin global pool for senior engineers who can read an unfamiliar codebase fast and diagnose under pressure. That skill is exactly what Corporate AI 365 automates the first pass of — without ever needing to see a live database to do it.

This is the part worth being precise about: Corporate AI 365 never hosts your code and never connects to a live database. It reasons over your source code and a scripted schema export you control. When a diagnosis genuinely needs live data to confirm, the AI writes a read-only query and hands it to your own developer to run — the result stays inside your organization. For a security or compliance review in a regulated Canadian sector like banking or healthcare, that's the sentence that ends the conversation early.

A fix that's governed, provable, and reversible

A plain-language report and a proposed fix aren't worth much without a trail that satisfies an audit. Every fix Corporate AI 365 proposes moves through real governance: Developer, QA, approval, and production, as actual git branches and pull requests, across GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or Azure DevOps. Every gate is a permission; every transition is logged. Your own CI confirms what shipped, and a full release can be reverted in one click if something's wrong. Because each diagnosis is cached against the exact issue text, code snapshot, and model used, re-running the same report produces the same answer — which is what makes an approval step mean something instead of being theater.

For a Manager or QA lead, that governed trail also feeds into Face Off, which scores developers, teams, and departments on real delivered work and gives an AI umpire's verdict on where the actual bottleneck sits — useful when the honest answer is process, not people.

None of this requires a bigger team or a rarer hire. It requires giving the developers you already have fewer reasons to be pulled out of flow, and giving everyone else in the company a way to report a problem without needing to speak engineer.

title: Your Runbook Drifted Since the Last Incident: Audit Alert Names, Permissions, and Step Intent in CI
summary:
Your Runbook Drifted Since the Last Incident: Audit Alert Names, Permissions, and Step Intent in CI

A runbook rarely fails because the idea behind it was wrong; it fails because something around it moved while nobody was looking. The alert got renamed during a dashboard cleanup, the rotation lost a cluster role in a permissions refactor, or the prose says "restart the pod" while the command quietly deletes the deployment. All three of those are mechanical, testable, and cheap to catch before the pager goes off — so why do we still discover them from a laptop at 3 a.m.?

Here is the workflow I keep coming back to: give every runbook step a small machine-readable block, then run three passes over it — alert-name resolution, permission proof, and a semantic check that the command actually matches the stated intent. The first two are deterministic and run in CI, and the third only needs a throwaway model endpoint.

Why runbooks rot quietly

Review culture is optimized for the day the runbook is written, not the six months after it. Docs get review comments about clarity, tone, and ordering, but almost nobody re-reads them when the alerting rules change or when the platform team tightens RBAC. That is why drift accumulates silently and surfaces only under pressure.

There are three drift classes worth separating, because they need different detectors:

  • Renamed or deleted alerts. The runbook references CheckoutLatencyP99High, but the rule is now checkout_latency_p99_high or lives in a different rule file entirely.
  • Revoked permissions. The step was authored by someone with cluster-admin, so it "worked" once; the on-call rotation only has namespace-scoped patch rights.
  • Prose that no longer matches the command. Someone edited the command during an incident and updated the title loosely, so the step now claims one outcome and produces another.

Give every step a machine-readable block

If you keep runbook steps as free-form prose, no tool can help you without an NLP project. Pick a boring convention instead: one ### heading per step, followed by a fenced runbook block of YAML. Humans still read the prose around it; the auditor reads the block.

### Checkout latency page

The p99 latency alert fires when the checkout API is slow but still serving traffic.

```runbook
alert: CheckoutLatencyP99High
namespace: prod
command: kubectl -n prod rollout restart deploy/checkout-api
requires:
  - patch deployments
intent: restart the checkout API pods so a bad in-memory cache is rebuilt
read_only: false
```

If the restart does not clear the alert within ten minutes, escalate per the contacts section.

That is it. One block per step, four fields that matter, and a requires list written in the same verb resource shape that kubectl auth can-i already understands.

Pass 1 — every alert name must resolve

The cheapest check is also the one that catches the most embarrassing failures. Parse the runbook, collect the alert fields, then parse your Prometheus rule files and confirm each name exists.

# alerts/checkout.yml
groups:
  - name: checkout
    rules:
      - alert: CheckoutLatencyP99High
        expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="checkout"}[5m]))) > 1.5
        for: 10m

Run promtool check rules alerts/checkout.yml first so you are comparing against syntactically valid rules, then compare the name sets yourself. A missing name is not a style nit; it means the person paged at 3 a.m. will search for an alert that no longer exists.

Pass 2 — prove the rotation can actually run the command

This is the check most teams skip, and it is the one that converts a runbook into something executable. kubectl auth can-i is a read-only self-check: it answers what the current identity may do, without changing anything. Run it with the rotation's credentials, not your admin kubeconfig — otherwise every probe returns yes and proves nothing.

# As the on-call identity, not as an admin:
kubectl auth can-i patch deployments -n prod
# yes  -> the step is runnable
# no   -> the runbook is fiction for anyone on rotation

Do the same for whatever the step actually touches. If a step shells into a bastion, run ssh -o BatchMode=yes bastion true and check the exit code. If it calls an internal API, hit a /healthz endpoint with the token the rotation holds. The point is to turn "we think this works" into a recorded yes or no.

Pass 3 — catch prose that lies about the command

Name resolution and permissions are binary, but intent mismatch is fuzzy, which is exactly where a model earns its keep. For each step, send the intent and the command and ask one narrow question: does this command plausibly achieve that intent? Keep the prompt boring and demand JSON, so the output is parseable rather than a paragraph of encouragement.

SEMANTIC_PROMPT = """You audit an on-call runbook step. Reply with JSON only.
{"mismatch": true|false, "reason": ""}
Set mismatch=true when the command does not plausibly achieve the stated intent."""

This is the AI usage I actually endorse during the current wave of AI fatigue: narrow, gated, reversible, and attached to a review step rather than a production action. It flags candidates; a human still deletes the step.

<p>I am labeling this as a reference implementation, not a battle-tested product: I have not run it against your cluster, and pass 2 is only as trustworthy as the identity you run it with.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Wire it into the handoff, not just CI
</h2>



<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight yaml"><code><span class="na">name</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s">runbook-audit</span>
<span class="na">on</span><span class="pi">:</span>
